Sequential counterfactual methods replace history items while controlling perturbation size and temporal dependencies; popularity-stratified research shows that item-frequency distributions affect offline conclusions. The sources support these ingredients, but do not establish a single standard popularity-matched substitution protocol. A practical synthesis: compute per-category frequencies exclusively from training interactions; freeze documented log-frequency or quantile bins, keeping equal-frequency ties together. Match within bins, optionally enforcing a log-frequency caliper and reporting residual imbalance. [Popularity-stratified evaluation](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/193202/), [temporal counterfactual histories](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/20/11176).

For reproducible diagnostics, sort eligible item IDs and use seeded sampling without replacement within each perturbed history. Exclude padding, the original item, retained history items and replacements already selected; document selection order because small pools can create order effects. A conservative timestamp proxy requires a replacement’s first observed training interaction to precede the replaced event. This establishes prior observation, not actual release date or continued availability. Full-training frequencies can still contain information from after that event; use prefix-only frequencies for a strictly historical sensitivity check, without changing benchmark splits. [Temporal-leakage study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11060).

Compare perturbation variants on identical users and positions where every variant has an eligible replacement: common support. Report paired prediction changes alongside attempted/matched counts, coverage by category, frequency bin and sequence position, pool sizes, and failure reasons. Never silently widen bins, insert unchanged histories as successful interventions, or treat failed matches as zero effects. Report unmatched interventions separately and state that matched-only conclusions apply to the retained subset; matching popularity alone does not establish causality. [Matching and common-support guidance](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2943670/).
